description:
This page is meant to be a one stop shop for all performance investigations in NRP.  From here you should be able to tell:

* Batch Manager Times
* Subscription Lock Times
* EG times (if available)

Filtering down to the operation or correlation id is available, but leaving those fields blank will also give the overall performance profile for a subscription in a given time frame

children.header:
This dashboard can help diagnose the following categories of issues:
* High delays from write transactions, due to either subscription lock or batch manager delays
* Partition wide issues with high read / write size
* High delays due to downstream services (when EG is available)

This dashboard cannot help diagnose deeper performance issues such as the following:
* Thread exhaustion issues
* Garbage collection and other transient .NET delays
* Blocked subscription locks / batch manager down issues

QOS table information is a good starting point to help see exactly what a customer is doing / if they claim what their issue is appears to actually be the issue.  Usually checking here is best to see what operations are taking the longest, how many of each given api call type we are receiving, etc.  Taking a look here can help identify exactly where to start your investigation on later tabs and try and find operation ids / correlation ids to filter by.

This tab is meant to try and pull the worst offending data points from each of the following categories to help provide operation ids and correlation ids to narrow your search with.  If you have already been given an operation id or correlation id to check you can probably skip this tab.  If all you have is a subscription, region and time frame then starting here is likely your best bet to figure out what may be going wrong.

Any times here over ~1000 indicate that an individual job / category of jobs are taking longer than they should on this subscription, and with a high enough volume of these high duration jobs the customers subscription could experience very high latency on write transactions.  These high durations can also cause throttling on incoming requests if we cant process them within 30s.

Most of our services high-throughput operations are no longer using subscription locks, but some operations like PutVmss still do and can sometimes take very long underneath this lock.  If times here are over ~10000 and there are more than one of these calls per minute it will likely cause high latency on customer write transactions and similar throttling exceptions as batch manager delays.

When one of our partitions reads too much data it can cause high GC delays, thread exhaustion and sometimes out of memory exceptions that cause the partition to failover.  This can appear to customers as operations that have been stuck in progress for tens to hundreds of minutes while our service is stuck in a loop reading too much data.  If any operations here are reading over 20mb checking the readsize for the given correlation id on the transaction stats tab is a good next step to see how much data is being read by all operations on that correlation id.

EG is an underutilized resource for investigating performance, most of the time because we are forced to rely on EG viewer to get latency information.  This page can pull this same EG latency information for NRP operations though, and so as long as the subscription is emitting EG logs we can pull this information.  This query only gets latency information one level down, meaning that it will only give a high level view of where operation time is going and can't break apart more detailed components of our background tasks other than information like which api call is being made to which service.  the OperationName can usually be found hardcoded into the operation source code, so if it is unclear what a given frame may be and needs further investigation it can usually be found by searching for it in our repo.
Here are some common EG operationName categories you will see and what they mean:
* Nrp Operation Name: this relates to time spent in the ExecuteAsync path of the given operation name.
* Nrp Operation Name - Async: this relates to time spent in the RunBackgroundTaskAsync path of the given operation name
* RnmClient.*: this relates to NRP code involved with calling Rnm + the api call time itself that is attributable to their service
* SlbClient.*: this relates to NRP involved in SLB goal state creation + the api call to SLB

children.helpText: Spikes here typically indicate poisonous jobs. One huge spike could cause all x jobs (typically 100) in a batch to time out or for a whole batch of jobs to be slow due to transitive blocking or the convoy effect.

Each column is split into the different percentiles by color. The default batch size is 100. Having a value of 100 across all queue types means there are lots of jobs in the Batch Manager and that it may be choking.

Worst performing non-tenant/VM/VMSS operations by duration. 
This graph samples the top 10.

children.header: Batch manager is our system for efficiently processing write transactions.  If batch manager is running slow it means that customers will experience high delays in having their calls accepted, long vm deployment times, and in extreme cases throttling due to an ability to process write transactions.  There are two main parts to determining whether batch manager is running slow for a subscription, the queue processing durations and the job durations.

Queue processing durations are how long write transaction jobs spend interacting with batch manager.  This includes all lock acquisition time, job execution time, and transaction commit time.  Determining exactly what the source of the times seen here is can be very difficult, but most of the time it is due to a high volume of high duration jobs.  If any of the queue durations here (except for those mentioning Ultra Low) are over 30000 ms then customers will experience throttling.  We use this value as a benchmark, and if times are lower we would consider batch manager healthy.  If the times are higher, looking at the durations and volume of the individual jobs is usually best to determine what the source of the delays are.

Job durations are measurements of exactly how long specific pieces of buisness logic are taking to execute in batch manger.  In an optimized workflow we would expect all the numbers here to be under 100ms in the p95, but customers usually wont notice any delays unless there is a high call volume (over 3k calls per min) or p50 job durations are somewhere in the 500-1000 ms range.  If some of these numbers are high in both count and p50 duration then they are likely responsible for the delay being seen.

Most operations in NRP don't use subscription lock anymore, but the ones that do tend to be the least optimized / unmaintained operations in the codebase.  This means we occasionally see unanticipated customer configurations hit delays here or data access layer regressions cause delays.  If it looks like these numbers are in the 10000-30000 ms range in the p50 then these locks are likely responsible for latency delays.

Debugging read / write information and the delays they cause can be very tricky to do.  This is because there are two main issues high read size can cause, transient delays or partition failovers.
* Delays from read size are a combination of GC pressure caused by reading large volumes of data and high cpu usage involved in deserializing this data.  Because many pieces of code that read have no concurrency control on them, this means that potentially hundreds to thousands of threads can be trying to read lots of data at once.  This can delay write transactions by making them compete for resources more with the other operations on the partition, make some networking calls non responsive while we read and cause transient delays for the whole partition.  
* Partition failovers can happen from OutOfMemoryException, but these are usually rarer than simply delays caused by reading.  OOM are usually only thrown when there's a combination of both high read size and logic that keeps the read data loaded in memory for a long time.  An example of a healthy read is a GetResources operation, where the data is read and then immediately released by GC because the operation has completed.  This poses little risk to partition health.  An unhealthy read example would be if an operation read 50mb of resource data at the beginning of its background task and proceeded to make a potentially 15 minute long api call to Rnm.  This data would remain in memory for the entire duration of the operation, leaving us vulnerable to a customer that may want to run this same thing hundreds of times concurrently which could crash our machine from loading too much data.  

Time frames are essential here to debugging, and if you have a correlation id that works best for tracking down exactly what a given update is attempting to read.

When evaluating how a subscription is performing one of the important metrics is this Exclusive Write Time Attribution.  A given subscription only has a certain amount of throughput it can handle, as write transactions are processed either through subscription lock or Resource Locking.  Even though on resource locking we run many write transactions in parallel, we have a limit of 20 parallel jobs running at once and so even this can create a bottleneck if the incoming load is higher than we can process.  

To figure out what is limiting a subscriptions write operation throughput we can look at this query to see what is holding the most of a subscriptions exclusive write time.  For subscription lock this will be the duration of the subscription lock, for resource locking it is the total time it took us to process a batch of parallel jobs divided by the level of parallelism we achieved, as we hold a subscription lock while we run those jobs in parallel.

This is sorted by the total duration a piece of logic is holding this exclusivity for, so to optimize a subsccriptions workload the most we should pay attention to the top pieces of logic and find why they are running slowly.
